title: The Explorer's Daughter
author: Kari Herbert
blurb: Watching a narwhal hunt in Greenland, Herbert weighs childhood memories against an adult understanding of Arctic survival.
source: Herbert writes about her experience watching a narwhal hunt in the Arctic
heading: The Explorer's Daughter - Kari Herbert
context: As a small child, Herbert lived, with her family, among the Inughuit people (sometimes called Inuits, or Eskimos) in the harsh environment of the Arctic. In 2002 she revisited the area, staying near Thule, a remote settlement in North Greenland. In this passage she writes about her experience of watching a hunt for the narwhal, a toothed whale, and what she thought and felt about it.

paragraphs.html: Two hours after the last of the hunters had returned and eaten, narwhal were spotted again, this time very close. Within an hour even those of us on shore could with the naked eye see the plumes of spray from the narwhal catching the light in a spectral play of colour. Two large pods of narwhal circled in the fjord, often looking as if they were going to merge, but always slowly, methodically passing each other by. Scrambling back up to the lookout I looked across the glittering kingdom in front of me and took a sharp intake of breath. The hunters were dotted all around the fjord. The evening light was turning butter-gold, glinting off man and whale and catching the soft billows of smoke from a lone hunter's pipe. From where we sat at the lookout it looked as though the hunters were close enough to touch the narwhal with their bare hands and yet they never moved. Distances are always deceptive in the Arctic, and I fell to wondering if the narwhal existed at all or were instead mischievous tricks of the shifting light. ...

The narwhal rarely stray from High Arctic waters, escaping only to the slightly more temperate waters towards the Arctic Circle in the dead of winter, but never entering the warmer southern seas. In summer the hunters of Thule are fortunate to witness the annual return of the narwhal to the Inglefield Fjord, on the side of which we now sat.

The narwhal ... is an essential contributor to the survival of the hunters in the High Arctic. The mattak or blubber of the whale is rich in necessary minerals and vitamins, and in a place where the climate prohibits the growth of vegetables or fruit, this rich source of vitamin C was the one reason that the Eskimos have never suffered from scurvy. ... For centuries the blubber of the whales was also the only source of light and heat, and the dark rich meat is still a valuable part of the diet for both man and dogs (a single narwhal can feed a team of dogs for an entire month). Its single ivory tusk, which can grow up to six feet in length, was used for harpoon tips and handles for other hunting implements (although the ivory was found to be brittle and not hugely satisfactory as a weapon), for carving protective tupilaks, and even as a central beam for their small ancient dwellings. Strangely, the tusk seems to have little use for the narwhal itself; they do not use the tusk to break through ice as a breathing hole, nor will they use it to catch or attack prey, but rather the primary use seems to be to disturb the top of the sea bed in order to catch Arctic halibut for which they have a particular predilection. Often the ends of their tusks are worn down or even broken from such usage.

The women clustered on the knoll of the lookout, binoculars pointing in every direction, each woman focusing on her husband or family member, occasionally spinning round at a small gasp or jump as one of the women saw a hunter near a narwhal. ... Each wife knew her husband instinctively and watched their progress intently; it was crucial to her that her husband catch a narwhal — it was part of their staple diet, and some of the mattak and meat could be sold to other hunters who hadn't been so lucky, bringing in some much-needed extra income. Every hunter was on the water. It was like watching a vast, waterborne game with the hunters spread like a net around the sound.

The narwhal ... are intelligent creatures, their senses are keen and they talk to one another under the water. Their hearing is particularly developed and they can hear the sound of a paddling kayak from a great distance. That ... was why the hunters had to sit so very still in the water.

One hunter was almost on top of a pair of narwhal, and they were huge. He gently picked up his harpoon and aimed — in that split second my heart leapt for both hunter and narwhal. I urged the man on in my head; he was so close, and so brave to attempt what he was about to do — he was miles from land in a flimsy kayak, and could easily be capsized and drowned. The hunter had no rifle, only one harpoon with two heads and one bladder. It was a foolhardy exercise and one that could only inspire respect. And yet at the same time my heart also urged the narwhal to dive, to leave, to survive.

This dilemma stayed with me the whole time that I was in Greenland. I understand the harshness of life in the Arctic and the needs of the hunters and their families to hunt and live on animals and sea mammals that we demand to be protected because of their beauty. And I know that one cannot afford to be sentimental in the Arctic. 'How can you possibly eat seal?' I have been asked over and over again. True, the images that bombarded us several years ago of men battering seals for their fur hasn't helped the issue of polar hunting, but the Inughuit do not kill seals using this method, nor do they kill for sport. They use every part of the animals they kill, and most of the food in Thule is still brought in by the hunter-gatherers and fishermen. Imported goods can only ever account for part of the food supply; there is still only one annual supply ship that makes it through the ice to Qaanaaq, and the small twice-weekly plane from West Greenland can only carry a certain amount of goods. Hunting is still an absolute necessity in Thule.

spectral-play.quote: the plumes of spray from the narwhal catching the light in a spectral play of colour
spectral-play.what: 'Spectral' means ghostly, so the spray shimmers like something from another world.
spectral-play.effect: Meeting the narwhal as magical before we meet them as prey makes the hunt harder to watch.

two-pods.quote: Two large pods of narwhal circled in the fjord, often looking as if they were going to merge, but always slowly, methodically passing each other by
two-pods.what: 'Slowly, methodically' makes the pods move like careful dancers who almost meet but never do.
two-pods.effect: The steady rhythm builds quiet suspense: we wait, just as the hunters wait.

glittering-kingdom.what: 'Kingdom' is a fairytale word, and 'glittering' adds the sparkle of treasure.
glittering-kingdom.effect: Readers who imagine the Arctic as an empty, frozen waste are made to see it as rich and precious.

sharp-intake.quote: took a sharp intake of breath
sharp-intake.what: Herbert shows her awe through a gasp, a reaction you cannot fake.
sharp-intake.effect: We share her amazement, and see that even someone who grew up here is still stunned.

butter-gold.quote: The evening light was turning butter-gold, glinting off man and whale and catching the soft billows of smoke from a lone hunter's pipe
butter-gold.what: Warm, homely 'butter-gold' light falls on 'man and whale' alike, joining them in one picture.
butter-gold.effect: Hunter and prey look equally at home, which makes the coming kill harder to judge.

close-enough.quote: From where we sat at the lookout it looked as though the hunters were close enough to touch the narwhal with their bare hands and yet they never moved
close-enough.what: 'And yet they never moved' turns the hunters' closeness into a long, tense wait.
close-enough.effect: Their stillness shows huge patience and self-control, and we feel the strain of it.

distances-deceptive.quote: Distances are always deceptive in the Arctic
distances-deceptive.what: 'Always' makes this general truth sound like knowledge Herbert has learned the hard way.
distances-deceptive.effect: We learn that this place has its own rules, and even our eyes cannot be trusted.

fell-wondering.quote: I fell to wondering if the narwhal existed at all or were instead mischievous tricks of the shifting light
fell-wondering.what: 'Mischievous' gives the light a teasing personality, as if the whales might be a trick.
fell-wondering.effect: This dreamlike mood will soon clash with the real business of killing a whale.

rarely-stray.quote: The narwhal rarely stray from High Arctic waters
rarely-stray.what: Herbert's tone turns calm and informative, like a nature guide.
rarely-stray.effect: Knowing the narwhal live only here makes their yearly return feel special, and vital to the hunters.

hunters-fortunate.quote: the hunters of Thule are fortunate to witness the annual return of the narwhal to the Inglefield Fjord
hunters-fortunate.what: 'Fortunate' and 'witness' make the narwhal's return sound like a gift to the hunters.
hunters-fortunate.effect: We are invited to see the hunt as the hunters do: a yearly event they are grateful for.

essential-contributor.quote: The narwhal ... is an essential contributor to the survival of the hunters in the High Arctic
essential-contributor.what: 'Contributor' makes the narwhal sound like a partner that gives something to the people.
essential-contributor.effect: 'Essential' and 'survival' frame her case for the hunt as life and death.

rich-minerals.quote: rich in necessary minerals and vitamins
rich-minerals.what: 'Necessary minerals and vitamins' sounds scientific and means the body cannot do without them.
rich-minerals.effect: It is harder to call the hunt cruel once we see that people's health depends on it.

climate-prohibits.quote: in a place where the climate prohibits the growth of vegetables or fruit, this rich source of vitamin C was the one reason that the Eskimos have never suffered from scurvy
climate-prohibits.what: Mattak supplied vitamin C, preventing scurvy (an illness caused by lacking it) where nothing grows.
climate-prohibits.effect: 'The one reason' leaves no other option: without the narwhal, people would have died.

for-centuries.quote: For centuries the blubber of the whales was also the only source of light and heat
for-centuries.what: 'For centuries' and 'the only source' show that whole lives once depended on the whale.
for-centuries.effect: Such an old way of life is harder to judge by modern Western standards.

valuable-diet.quote: the dark rich meat is still a valuable part of the diet for both man and dogs (a single narwhal can feed a team of dogs for an entire month)
valuable-diet.what: 'Still' shows people depend on the narwhal today.
valuable-diet.effect: One narwhal feeding a dog team for a month is easy to picture and hard to argue with.

ivory-tusk.quote: Its single ivory tusk, which can grow up to six feet in length
ivory-tusk.what: 'Six feet' is the height of a tall man, and 'single ivory' sounds rare and precious.
ivory-tusk.effect: Wonder sits beside usefulness, as Herbert moves straight on to the tusk's practical uses.

strangely-tusk.quote: Strangely, the tusk seems to have little use for the narwhal itself
strangely-tusk.what: 'Strangely' adds Herbert's own puzzled reaction to the facts.
strangely-tusk.effect: Her curiosity makes the facts feel human and keeps the narwhal a little mysterious.

worn-broken.quote: Often the ends of their tusks are worn down or even broken from such usage
worn-broken.what: 'Even broken' stresses how hard the narwhal use their tusks.
worn-broken.effect: They seem like real working animals with scars, balancing the magical opening.

women-clustered.quote: The women clustered on the knoll of the lookout, binoculars pointing in every direction
women-clustered.what: Herbert turns to the women on shore, 'clustered' together with binoculars 'pointing in every direction'.
women-clustered.effect: Every hunter matters to someone, so the whole community is caught up in the hunt.

each-woman.quote: each woman focusing on her husband or family member, occasionally spinning round at a small gasp or jump as one of the women saw a hunter near a narwhal
each-woman.what: Small actions like 'spinning round' and 'a small gasp' show the women's nerves.
each-woman.effect: Their tension spreads to us, and we start to want the hunters to succeed.

knew-instinctively.quote: Each wife knew her husband instinctively and watched their progress intently
knew-instinctively.what: 'Instinctively' suggests each wife knows her husband without thinking, and 'intently' shows her focus.
knew-instinctively.effect: A failed hunt would now hurt families we care about.

crucial-catch.quote: it was crucial to her that her husband catch a narwhal — it was part of their staple diet, and some of the mattak and meat could be sold to other hunters who hadn't been so lucky, bringing in some much-needed extra income
crucial-catch.what: 'Crucial' is explained twice over: the catch feeds the family and earns 'much-needed' money.
crucial-catch.effect: We see that these families have little, and hunting is how they make a living.

waterborne-game.quote: It was like watching a vast, waterborne game with the hunters spread like a net around the sound
waterborne-game.what: Hunters 'spread like a net' suggests teamwork, with each man in place.
waterborne-game.effect: Yet a net also traps, so we admire the hunters and pity the narwhal at once.

intelligent-creatures.quote: The narwhal ... are intelligent creatures, their senses are keen and they talk to one another under the water
intelligent-creatures.what: 'Intelligent' and 'talk to one another' are qualities we usually give to people.
intelligent-creatures.effect: The narwhal seem almost human, so we share Herbert's unease about killing them.

hearing-developed.quote: Their hearing is particularly developed and they can hear the sound of a paddling kayak from a great distance
hearing-developed.what: Hearing a paddle 'from a great distance' makes the narwhal very hard to catch.
hearing-developed.effect: The hunt feels closer to a fair contest that needs real skill.

why-still.quote: That ... was why the hunters had to sit so very still in the water
why-still.what: This explains why the hunters in paragraph 1 'never moved'.
why-still.effect: What looked strange now shows the hunters' skill, giving us a small moment of discovery.

split-second.quote: in that split second my heart leapt for both hunter and narwhal
split-second.what: One 'split second' holds two opposite feelings, for 'both hunter and narwhal'.
split-second.effect: This is the emotional centre of the passage, and we may feel torn too.

urged-on.quote: I urged the man on in my head
urged-on.what: Herbert cheers silently, 'in my head', showing her first loyalty is to the hunter.
urged-on.effect: We are drawn to his side too, so her later wish for the narwhal is more striking.

brave-attempt.quote: he was so close, and so brave to attempt what he was about to do — he was miles from land in a flimsy kayak, and could easily be capsized and drowned
brave-attempt.what: Herbert piles up dangers, from a 'flimsy kayak' to 'capsized and drowned'.
brave-attempt.effect: A man risking his life to feed his family is hard to condemn.

no-rifle.quote: The hunter had no rifle, only one harpoon with two heads and one bladder
no-rifle.what: 'No rifle, only one harpoon' suggests he has a single chance.
no-rifle.effect: Success depends on skill alone, so our respect for the hunter grows.

foolhardy-respect.quote: It was a foolhardy exercise and one that could only inspire respect
foolhardy-respect.what: 'Foolhardy' (reckless) and 'respect' let her hold both views at once.
foolhardy-respect.effect: Her honest mixed feelings make her seem fair, a balance she keeps all through the passage.

yet-same-time.quote: And yet at the same time my heart also urged the narwhal to dive, to leave, to survive
yet-same-time.what: 'And yet' turns her feelings round, and three verbs build to 'survive'.
yet-same-time.effect: This mirrors her cheering of the hunter, giving both sides equal weight.

dilemma-stayed.quote: This dilemma stayed with me the whole time that I was in Greenland
dilemma-stayed.what: She names her feeling a 'dilemma' (a choice between two hard options) that lasted 'the whole time'.
dilemma-stayed.effect: The passage turns from the hunt to reflection on a problem with no easy answer.

understand-harshness.quote: I understand the harshness of life in the Arctic and the needs of the hunters and their families to hunt and live on animals and sea mammals that we demand to be protected because of their beauty
understand-harshness.what: Herbert sets the hunters' 'needs' against what 'we demand', meaning Western readers.
understand-harshness.effect: Protecting animals 'because of their beauty' is easy when your survival does not depend on them.

cannot-sentimental.quote: And I know that one cannot afford to be sentimental in the Arctic
cannot-sentimental.what: 'Cannot afford' uses money language: soft feelings are a luxury the Arctic cannot pay for.
cannot-sentimental.effect: It hints that her readers' feelings come from a comfortable life.

how-eat-seal.quote: 'How can you possibly eat seal?' I have been asked over and over again
how-eat-seal.what: 'Possibly' carries the critics' disgust, and 'over and over again' her weariness.
how-eat-seal.effect: Raising the reader's likely objection before answering it makes her argument feel fair.

true-images.quote: True, the images that bombarded us several years ago of men battering seals for their fur hasn't helped the issue of polar hunting
true-images.what: 'True' admits the critics have a point: a concession (agreeing with part of the other side).
true-images.effect: Admitting this earns our trust, so we are ready to hear her answer.

not-kill-method.quote: but the Inughuit do not kill seals using this method, nor do they kill for sport
not-kill-method.what: 'But' turns the argument: the Inughuit never use that method or kill 'for sport'.
not-kill-method.effect: We are asked to stop lumping all hunting together, because the Inughuit hunt to live.

use-every-part.quote: They use every part of the animals they kill
use-every-part.what: 'Every part' stresses that nothing is thrown away.
use-every-part.effect: Wasting nothing shows respect for the animal, and may make Western readers think about their own waste.

food-brought.quote: most of the food in Thule is still brought in by the hunter-gatherers and fishermen
food-brought.what: 'Still' shows that hunters provide most of Thule's food today.
food-brought.effect: We cannot dismiss the hunt as an old custom when people rely on it for meals.

imported-goods.quote: Imported goods can only ever account for part of the food supply; there is still only one annual supply ship that makes it through the ice to Qaanaaq, and the small twice-weekly plane from West Greenland can only carry a certain amount of goods
imported-goods.what: 'One annual supply ship' and a 'small twice-weekly plane' show how cut off Thule is.
imported-goods.effect: These hard facts prove imported food alone could never feed the town.

absolute-necessity.quote: Hunting is still an absolute necessity in Thule
absolute-necessity.what: 'Absolute' leaves no doubt, and 'still' echoes her present-day facts.
absolute-necessity.effect: After all her mixed feelings, she ends on a clear verdict: the hunters' needs come first.

mattak.meaning: The fatty skin and blubber of a whale.
mattak.note: An Inughuit word. Mattak is rich in the vitamins and minerals people need to survive in the Arctic.
mattak.effect: Using the local word shows respect for Inughuit culture. It reminds us this is a traditional way of life.

tupilaks.meaning: Carved figures or charms believed to have protective powers.
tupilaks.note: Traditional Inuit carvings thought to have spiritual or magical power.
tupilaks.effect: Narwhal tusk was used for sacred objects too. The animal matters to the culture as well as to survival.

predilection.meaning: A preference or special liking for something.
predilection.note: From Latin, meaning 'to choose beforehand'. Here it means the narwhal's fondness for halibut.
predilection.effect: This formal word adds authority to her facts. It also adds a touch of humour, as if the narwhal were a fussy eater.

overview.heading: Why Herbert wrote this
overview.intro: Herbert has several purposes, and they shift as the passage goes on.

points.label: To explain Arctic survival
points.text: "an essential contributor to the survival" shows that hunting is a matter of life and death.

points.label: To challenge Western views
points.text: "How can you possibly eat seal?" shows she is answering Western critics directly.

points.label: To share her mixed feelings
points.text: "This dilemma stayed with me" shows that she feels torn herself.

overview.heading: Who she is writing for
overview.intro: Herbert writes for several kinds of reader.

points.label: Readers new to the Arctic
points.text: "Distances are always deceptive in the Arctic" shows her teaching outsiders how this place works.

points.label: Critics of Arctic hunting
points.text: "I have been asked over and over again" shows she is replying to criticism she hears often.

points.label: Curious readers
points.text: Facts such as "a single narwhal can feed a team of dogs for an entire month" reward readers who want to learn.

overview.heading: How her tone changes
overview.intro: Herbert's voice changes as the passage moves on.

points.label: Wonder and awe
points.text: "took a sharp intake of breath" shows her amazement at the beauty of the scene.

points.label: Calm teacher
points.text: "intelligent creatures" shows a clear, factual tone as she explains the narwhal.

points.label: Torn observer
points.text: "my heart leapt for both hunter and narwhal" shows her split loyalties.

points.label: Firm defender
points.text: "one cannot afford to be sentimental" shows a firm tone as she defends the Inughuit.

overview.heading: Language choices
overview.intro: Herbert's word choices shape how we see the Arctic.

points.label: Magical imagery
points.text: "spectral play of colour" and "glittering kingdom" make the Arctic seem like a fairytale world.

points.label: Colour and light
points.text: "butter-gold" is a warm, homely colour that makes the evening scene feel soft and calm.

points.label: Simile
points.text: "like watching a vast, waterborne game" presents the hunt as a skilled, organised contest.

points.label: Inughuit words
points.text: "mattak" and "tupilaks" are local words that show respect for Inughuit culture.

overview.heading: How it is organised
overview.intro: The order of ideas takes the reader from wonder to understanding.

points.label: Beauty to necessity
points.text: The passage opens with magical description, then moves to the hard facts of survival.

points.label: Turning point
points.text: "And yet at the same time" marks the moment her feelings split between hunter and narwhal.

points.label: Reflection and argument
points.text: After "This dilemma stayed with me", she turns to answering critics and defending the hunt.

points.label: Final emphasis
points.text: "Hunting is still an absolute necessity" ends the passage on a short, certain statement.
